title: De diuinatione daemonum
author: Augustine

passages.original: cum igitur tam longe ante praedictum esset atque conscriptum, ut alia interim taceam, illud, quod Sophonias propheta dicit: praeualebit dominus aduersus eos et exterminabit omnes deos gentium terrae, et adorabunt eum unusquisque de loco suo, omnes insulae gentium, aut non credebant ista sibi euentura, qui in templis gentium colebantur, et haec ideo per suos uates ac fanaticos frequentare noluerunt — sicut eorum poeta Iunonem inducit non omni modo credentem, quae de Turni morte Iuppiter dixerat: Iuno autem ab istis potestas aeria praedicatur, quae apud Virgilium sic loquitur: nunc manet insontem grauis exitus, aut ego ueri uana feror. quod ut o potius formidine falsa ludar et in Melius tua, qui potes, orsa reflectas! — aut ergo ista sibi, quae per prophetas praedicta nouerant, posse accidere daemones, hoc est potestates aeriae, dubitabant et propterea praedicationem eorum celebrare noluerunt — et hinc intellegendum est quales sint — aut, cum ea uentura certissime scirent, ideo per sua templa tacuerunt, ne iam tunc inciperent ab hominibus intellegentibus deseri atque contemni, quod de templorum et simulacrorum suorum futura euersione eis prophetis adtestarentur, qui eos coli prohibebant.
passages.english: Since, therefore, so long beforehand it had been foretold and written down (to say nothing of other things in the meantime) what the prophet Zephaniah says: "The Lord will prevail against them and will destroy all the gods of the nations of the earth, and they will worship him, each from his own place, all the islands of the nations," either those who were worshipped in the temples of the nations did not believe that these things would happen to them, and for that reason were unwilling to make them widely known through their seers and frenzied devotees (just as their poet presents Juno as not wholly believing what Jupiter had said about the death of Turnus; and Juno is proclaimed by these people to be an aerial power, who in Virgil speaks thus: "Now a grievous end awaits the guiltless man, or I am carried far astray from the truth. But oh, may I rather be mocked by a false fear, and may you, who are able, turn your undertakings to something better!"); either, then, the demons, that is, the aerial powers, doubted that these things, which they knew had been foretold through the prophets, could happen to them, and for that reason were unwilling to publicize the prophets' proclamation (and from this it should be understood what sort of beings they are); or else, though they knew most certainly that these things would come, they kept silent in their temples for this reason: so that they would not begin already then to be abandoned and despised by people of understanding, because they would be bearing witness, concerning the future overthrow of their temples and images, to those prophets who forbade them to be worshipped.
passages.notes: The Zephaniah quotation is Zeph. 2:11. The Virgil quotation is Aeneid 10.630–632. "in Melius" is read as "in melius"; the capital M appears to be a scanning or typographical error. The sentence is an anacoluthon: the first "aut" (either) is resumed after the parenthesis as "aut ergo" (either, then), and the translation keeps that repetition.
